question: Can per-sample local loss gradients be sparsely reconstructed from low-rank directions in parameter space that correspond to causally relevant model circuits?

key_findings.claim: Local Loss Landscape Decomposition learns low-rank parameter directions whose sparse combinations reconstruct gradients of output divergence relative to reference outputs.
key_findings.evidence: L3D factorizes transforms between parameter-gradient space and a subnetwork basis, applies batch Top-K sparse reconstruction, and represents each learned direction with Tucker-decomposed parameter tensors. Moving the original weights along a learned direction provides the causal intervention test.

key_findings.claim: Across progressively harder toy models, learned directions mostly recover known feature-specific or correlated-group computations, including superposed and higher-rank circuits.
key_findings.evidence: The circuit-superposition task achieves 6.4% gradient reconstruction loss and recovered coefficients highly correlate with the ground-truth matrix. In the nonlinear squared-input task, interventions primarily change outputs for the samples associated with the chosen subnetwork, though leakage grows for large moves.

key_findings.claim: Real-model decompositions yield suggestive human-interpretable clusters but do not yet provide faithful, complete circuits.
key_findings.evidence: For TinyStories-8M attention block 7, 100 subnetworks leave 40% reconstruction error and examples are cherry-picked for inspection. MobileNetV3 also has many dead circuits, reported at 40%; interpretations are based mainly on top affected texts, tokens, or images rather than independently specified behaviors.

method.core_idea: Decompose a model's local per-sample output-loss gradients into a sparse dictionary of low-rank parameter directions and treat those directions as candidate circuits.
method.mechanism: For sample/reference pairs, L3D computes a divergence gradient at fixed weights, learns input/output transforms with a Top-K reconstruction objective, and constrains dictionary elements through low-rank Tucker factors. Circuit relevance is measured by projected gradients and tested by finite parameter interventions.
assumptions: Only a sparse subset of parameter-space mechanisms is active for each sample.
Local first-order gradients approximate the effect of finite parameter moves.
Mechanisms admit low-rank parameter representations despite circuit superposition.
A subnetwork's affected examples and logits are sufficient evidence for a useful circuit interpretation.

techniques.role: Reconstructs paired-output divergence gradients with a small active set of candidate subnetworks.
Makes dictionary directions tractable by imposing low parameter-tensor rank.
Tests whether moving along one component selectively changes its associated samples.

evaluations.setting: Toy feature and circuit-superposition models with known mechanisms
evaluations.metric: gradient reconstruction, ground-truth direction recovery, and intervention selectivity
evaluations.result: L3D recovers feature-aligned directions; the circuit-superposition example reports 6.4% reconstruction loss and high recovered-coefficient correlation.
evaluations.baseline: Known generating subnetworks and decompositions with varied rank/component count.

evaluations.metric: reconstruction error and qualitative affected-token examples
evaluations.result: One hundred subnetworks leave about 40% reconstruction error; selected components align with phrases, grammar, or preceding subjects.
evaluations.baseline: No quantitative activation-decomposition or circuit-discovery baseline.

evaluations.metric: top affected images/logits and dead-component fraction
evaluations.result: Some components have coherent visual associations, but about 40% are dead and interpretation is qualitative.

limitations: Author-stated: local linear attribution can fail for large moves in a nonconvex loss landscape.
Author-stated: real-model decompositions have high reconstruction error, dead circuits, expensive gradient data, and unresolved hyperparameter choices.
Author-stated: there is no settled definition of a circuit, including whether ubiquitous scaffolding should count.
Reviewer inference: cherry-picked top examples do not establish component faithfulness, completeness, or human-independent interpretability.
failure_modes: Dense or highly interfering computation violates Top-K circuit sparsity.
A local direction changes unrelated behavior after a finite intervention.
Extra dictionary capacity becomes dead components or splits one mechanism arbitrarily.
Reference-output choice changes which gradients and therefore which circuits are recovered.
reusable_insights: Parameter-space dictionaries can complement activation features by exposing weights that causally move outputs.
Ground-truth circuit benchmarks should test both reconstruction and off-target intervention effects.
Low-rank factorization and sparse activation are separate assumptions and should be ablated independently.
open_questions: Can L3D scale from one block to whole large language models without storing prohibitive per-sample gradients?
How stable are learned circuits across seeds, reference distributions, ranks, and Top-K values?
Do L3D-restricted fine-tunes outperform activation steering or pruning on held-out behavior controls?

competitive_landscape.title: Interpretability in Parameter Space: Minimizing Mechanistic Description Length with Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition
competitive_landscape.difference: APD decomposes the model parameters themselves subject to faithfulness, sparse use, and simple mechanisms. L3D decomposes local paired-output gradients and therefore need not reconstruct the original parameter vector, trading global faithfulness for direct sample-specific attribution.

competitive_landscape.title: A Tale of Two Circuits: Grokking as Competition of Sparse and Dense Subnetworks
competitive_landscape.difference: The grokking study identifies task-specific sparse and dense algorithms through mechanistic analysis and ablation. L3D is an unsupervised general decomposition intended to recover multiple sparsely active circuits without first knowing the task algorithm.

competitive_landscape.title: Does Circuit Analysis Interpretability Scale? Evidence from Multiple Choice Capabilities in Chinchilla
competitive_landscape.difference: That work uses activation patching and component attribution to identify task circuits in a 70B model. L3D instead searches low-rank parameter directions and is architecture-agnostic, but has only qualitative real-model evidence at much smaller scale.

competitive_landscape.title: NeuroSurgeon: A Toolkit for Subnetwork Analysis
competitive_landscape.difference: NeuroSurgeon learns or evaluates masks over existing network units for behavior-specific subnetworks. L3D permits superposed, non-axis-aligned low-rank directions and learns an unsupervised dictionary from gradient structure.

novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference after comparison: L3D's distinctive choice is sparse decomposition of paired-output local gradients into non-axis-aligned, low-rank parameter directions. Toy recovery is convincing, but its real-model evidence is exploratory and materially weaker than the claim of identifying reliable circuits.
reviewer_notes: The full method, toy hierarchy, interventions, complete real-model examples, and discussion were reviewed. Primary records for APD, grokking circuits, Chinchilla circuit analysis, and NeuroSurgeon were checked on 2026-08-23.
